ocar.opportunity: How a network’s wiring and geometry constrain the dynamics it can support is still poorly understood, even in the fully mapped C. elegans nervous system.
ocar.challenge: Computational studies often simulate a named circuit in isolation, so it is unclear whether the signaling paths that appear in that reduced network still exist once the same cells sit inside the full connectome.
ocar.action: In Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2021), George, Puppo, and Silva simulate emergent dynamics on the known C. elegans connectome with a local-interaction model that does not depend on cell-intrinsic biophysics, stimulating the chemosensory neuron ASEL in a feeding circuit both in isolation and embedded in the whole worm.
ocar.resolution: Contralateral ventral (VB) and dorsal (DB) motor-neuron activations emerge that are qualitatively similar to rhythmic firing associated with locomotion. Using Temporal Sequences (TSeq)—time-ordered walks of signals on the graph—they find that only 5% of TSeq are preserved between the isolated feeding network and its embedded counterpart; 95% of isolated-network pathways are absent when the circuit is embedded.
ocar.future_work: The authors treat the result as a caution for computational studies of isolated neurobiological circuits. They also define Basis TSeqs (repeating versus one-time sequences) as a way to compress cyclic walks, but they do not claim a unique extraction algorithm.

summaries.beginner: A wiring diagram can be run as a simple simulation to see what activity patterns it can produce. This team finds that a feeding-circuit simulation in the worm looks locomotion-like, but almost all of the signaling paths change once that circuit is placed back inside the full nervous system.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience (2021), George, Puppo, and Silva stimulate ASEL in a known C. elegans feeding circuit both in isolation and embedded in the full connectome, using a model in which local interactions among connected neurons generate global dynamics without cell-intrinsic biophysical detail. Contralateral VB and DB motor-neuron activations emerge that they interpret as qualitatively similar to rhythmic locomotion patterns, which they take as evidence of purposeful structural wiring. An analytic framework of Temporal Sequences (TSeq) shows that only 5% of isolated-network signaling paths survive embedding; 95% do not. Code-level Basis TSeqs split repeating (cycle-derived) from one-time walks.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists a 2020 bioRxiv record; the extract is the March 2021 Frontiers article (doi 10.3389/fnsys.2021.564124). Dynamics are “plausible” simulations, not electrophysiology. Similarity to locomotion is qualitative. The 5%/95% TSeq comparison is between one isolated feeding network and its embedded counterpart under this model, not a general theorem about all reduced circuits. “Purposeful wiring” is the authors’ interpretation.

plain_language_summary: A wiring diagram can be run as a simple simulation to see what activity patterns it can produce. This team finds that a feeding-circuit simulation in the worm looks locomotion-like, but almost all of the signaling paths change once that circuit is placed back inside the full nervous system.

ocar.opportunity: A dense reconstruction of the adult Drosophila central brain makes it possible to treat a real insect brain as a directed, synapse-weighted graph rather than a sparse sample of connections.
ocar.challenge: Even with a dense connectome it is unclear which graph statistics are like human-designed logic, which differ across compartments, and which depend on unreconstructed biology such as gap junctions and neuromodulators.
ocar.action: In a May 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Scheffer analyzes the hemibrain as a directed graph with edge weights equal to synapse counts, reporting metrics for the sample as a whole and for computational compartments.
ocar.resolution: The volume contains around 25,000 neurons and about 20 million chemical synapses (21,662 uncropped traced neurons; 4,495 large but cropped). Neurons average 153 inputs and 153 outputs. Wiring is not random; compartments differ in all measured characteristics; paths are short compared with man-made circuits; connection strengths look like a power law with an exponential tail, unlike measured mammalian connections; cliques and many-to-one motifs are present; electrical response is strongly determined by compartment structure; and there is evidence for efficient packing.
ocar.future_work: Scheffer calls for whole-brain and ventral-nerve-cord analyses, additional specimens and species, and inclusion of neuromodulators, receptors, gap junctions, glia, and cell biology that this connectome omits.

summaries.beginner: A nearly complete wiring diagram of part of a fruit-fly’s central brain can be treated like a directed map of who talks to whom. This preprint reports that fly neurons have many inputs and outputs, paths are short, compartments differ, and the wiring is not random.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint posted 20 May 2020, Scheffer treats the Drosophila hemibrain as a directed, synapse-count-weighted graph. The reconstruction comprises about 25,000 neurons and about 20 million chemical synapses, including 21,662 uncropped traced neurons and 4,495 large (≥1000 connections) cropped cells. Reported conclusions include an average of 153 inputs and outputs, non-random wiring, compartment differences, short paths, a power-law-like strength distribution with an exponential tail, non-uniform strong connections, cliques and many-to-one motifs, compartment-determined electrical response, and evidence for efficient packing.
summaries.advanced: This is an unreviewed preprint that consolidates some analyses already in the hemibrain paper with new ones. Synapse count is treated as connection strength, which the author flags as an approximation. Cropped neurons and the volume boundary bias degree and path statistics. Gap junctions, neuromodulators, and glia are absent. “Electrical response” here is a graph-derived claim, not a new physiology experiment in this extract.

plain_language_summary: A nearly complete wiring diagram of part of a fruit-fly’s central brain can be treated like a directed map of who talks to whom. This preprint reports that fly neurons have many inputs and outputs, paths are short, compartments differ, and the wiring is not random.

ocar.opportunity: The developing C. elegans connectome has a rich club in a small-world architecture, but standard network statistics miss weakly connected motifs such as topological cavities that may support segregated computation.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear whether the growing connectome’s topology is a robust developmental feature, whether it is explained by simple growth models, and how sensitive it is to errors in birth times and missing synapses.
ocar.action: Helm, Blevins, and Bassett (bioRxiv/arXiv, 2020–2021) use persistent homology to track topological cavities as neurons are added in developmental birth order, and they test robustness with surrogate connectomes that add edges and jitter birth times.
ocar.resolution: Growing topology is relatively robust to birth-time noise and is not captured by similar growth models. In the PDF abstract, the growing topology is particularly insensitive to exact motor-neuron birth times. Sensitivity analyses (1,000 surrogates adding 800 connections and reassigning birth times within reported error: 10% embryonic, 2% later; about 10% of connections presumed missing) yield qualitatively similar Betti curves that remain statistically distinct from the reported connectome (p < 0.001).
ocar.future_work: The authors anticipate that cavity-tracking measurements will help build more accurate models of neuronal development. Wiring-cost-constrained surrogates shrink quantitative gaps but still differ from the reported curve.

summaries.beginner: As a worm’s neurons are born, the wiring diagram grows a shape that ordinary network scores can miss. This study tracks holes in that growing graph and finds the shape is fairly robust to noisy birth times and is not explained by simple growth models.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv (doi 10.1101/2020.12.31.424985; arXiv:2101.00065v2, August 2021), Helm, Blevins, and Bassett apply persistent homology to the C. elegans connectome grown in neuron birth order. They report that developing topology is robust to birth-time perturbation, is not captured by standard growth models, and—in this PDF version—is particularly insensitive to exact motor-neuron birth times. One thousand surrogates that add 800 edges and jitter birth times within published margins (10% embryonic, 2% later) keep the qualitative Betti-curve shape, with more cavities but p < 0.001 distance from the original curves; a wiring-cost-constrained variant reduces the quantitative gap.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract says topology is particularly sensitive to a small set of predominantly motor neurons; the PDF abstract says particularly insensitive to motor-neuron birth times—this card follows the PDF. Surrogate tests reject a “trivial perturbation” null but do not prove biological robustness of every cavity. Birth times and the connectome inherit White/Varshney-era incompleteness (about 10% missing connections assumed). Persistent homology of a growing graph depends on node order and edge set.

plain_language_summary: As a worm’s neurons are born, the wiring diagram grows a shape that ordinary network scores can miss. This study tracks holes in that growing graph and finds the shape is fairly robust to noisy birth times and is not explained by simple growth models.

ocar.opportunity: The complete C. elegans wiring diagram can be read as an information-processing network from roughly 90 sensory neurons through about 80 interneurons to about 120 motor neurons.
ocar.challenge: Highly recurrent interneuron connectivity hides whether feedforward sensory-to-motor flow actually bottlenecks through a small core, and whether that core matches other notions of hub neurons such as the rich club.
ocar.action: In PLoS Computational Biology (2020), Sabrin, Wei, van den Heuvel, and Dovrolis apply an “hourglass effect” analysis to the feedforward flow from sensory to motor neurons, separating feedforward from feedback paths.
ocar.resolution: Feedforward flow traverses a waist of 10–15 interneurons that largely overlap the previously identified rich club. The core is mostly stable whether chemical synapses are used alone or with gap junctions, and for the complete network they list 12 core cells (AVAL/R, AVBL/R, AVEL/R, PVCL/R, AIBR, AVDR, DVA, VD01), 10 of which were also synaptic-network cores. They analogize the waist to an encoder–decoder information bottleneck.
ocar.future_work: The authors frame the core as integrating sensory modalities before driving higher circuits; relating hourglass membership to physiology remains an experimental task. Data and code are at github.com/kmsabrin/hourglass-celegans.

summaries.beginner: Information entering a worm’s sensors has to reach muscles through a tangle of interneurons. This paper finds that the useful forward paths squeeze through a small set of about a dozen cells that were already known as a densely linked “rich club.”
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2020), Sabrin and colleagues treat the C. elegans connectome as an information-processing network (~90 sensory, ~80 inter, ~120 motor neurons) and apply hourglass analysis to feedforward sensory-to-motor paths. They report a waist of 10–15 interneurons overlapping the rich club, robust to how feedforward versus feedback is separated and largely unchanged when gap junctions are added. Table 3 lists 12 core neurons in the complete network (AVAL covering 0.29 of new paths, then AVAR 0.23, AVBL 0.16, AVBR 0.11, and others). They compare this bottleneck to encoder–decoder artificial nets.
summaries.advanced: Hourglass membership is a path-coverage statistic on an abstracted feedforward graph, not a measured information bottleneck in living worms. Overlap with rich-club, closeness-centrality, and connector-hub lists is correlative. Core lists depend on the path set (e.g., SP+2). Encoder–decoder language is an analogy. Results inherit connectome polarity and completeness conventions.

plain_language_summary: Information entering a worm’s sensors has to reach muscles through a tangle of interneurons. This paper finds that the useful forward paths squeeze through a small set of about a dozen cells that were already known as a densely linked “rich club.”

ocar.opportunity: Serotonergic neurons project widely and modulate many behaviors, but their connectivity has not been mapped at single-cell resolution through a whole brain.
ocar.challenge: A single identified serotonergic cell (the CSDn) spans several olfactory regions, so glomerulus-to-glomerulus differences, local versus projection targets, and non-olfactory inputs cannot be read from light-level anatomy alone.
ocar.action: In a February 2020 bioRxiv preprint (cataloged as Journal of Neuroscience), Coates, Calle-Schuler, Helmick, Knotts, Martik, Salman, Warner, Valla, Bock, and Dacks reconstruct CSDn synapses in a whole-brain EM volume of a female Drosophila.
ocar.resolution: In the antennal lobe the CSDn receives glomerulus-specific input and preferentially targets distinct local-interneuron subtypes rather than matching output to each glomerulus. Wiring logic differs in the lateral horn, where connectivity is more distributed and aligned with presumptive transmitter content of principal cells; the CSDn does not keep the same synaptic relationship with individual projection neurons that span AL and LH. Protocerebral neurons provide abundant non-olfactory synaptic input.
ocar.future_work: The study is offered as a ground plan for heterogeneous modulatory effects; physiology of the identified partners and generalization beyond this single neuron and specimen are left open.

summaries.beginner: A serotonin cell can wander through many smell-processing areas, so it is hard to know whom it actually talks to. This EM reconstruction of one identified fly neuron shows different wiring rules in different regions and strong input from outside olfaction.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint posted 25 February 2020 (catalog journal: Journal of Neuroscience), Coates and colleagues map the CSDn in a female Drosophila whole-brain EM volume. Within the antennal lobe they report glomerulus-specific input and preferential targeting of local interneuron subtypes; across the AL and lateral horn the same CSDn does not preserve its relationship with individual spanning projection neurons, and LH connectivity is more distributed by transmitter class. They also identify protocerebral neurons that provide abundant synaptic input. The significance framing is a single-cell account of serotonergic modulation in olfaction plus novel extrinsic drive.
summaries.advanced: The extract is the bioRxiv version of a paper cataloged as Journal of Neuroscience. Results are from one female brain and one identified neuron. Transmitter assignments for LH partners are presumptive. Connectivity is not a functional map of serotonin release or receptors. Polyadic insect synapses and proofreading completeness of the volume limit partner lists.

plain_language_summary: A serotonin cell can wander through many smell-processing areas, so it is hard to know whom it actually talks to. This EM reconstruction of one identified fly neuron shows different wiring rules in different regions and strong input from outside olfaction.

ocar.opportunity: Large biomedical volumes have too little expert label to train strong deep models, so active learning that picks the next images to annotate is a practical way to stretch a limited budget.
ocar.challenge: Query-suggestion networks trained only on the small labeled set become poorly matched to the harder unlabeled volume, so they stop choosing representative examples.
ocar.action: In ECCV (2020), Lin, Wei, Jang, Zhou, Chen, Wang, Schalek, Berger, Matejek, Kamentsky, Peleg, Haehn, Jones, Parag, Lichtman, and Pfister add an unsupervised feature stream trained on all raw images to a supervised stream, and they wrap the method in an end-to-end active-learning loop for 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation.
ocar.resolution: They curate what they describe as the largest connectomics dataset with dense synapse and mitochondria annotation. On that set the method outperforms previous state-of-the-art by 3.1% (synapse) and 3.8% (mitochondria) in region-of-interest proposal accuracy, and it also outperforms prior approaches on CIFAR-10 under the same limited annotation budget. In a synapse ablation, initial ROI accuracy is 0.762; annotating 4.46% of instances at random would add about 0.01, while their clustering module adds about 0.08.
ocar.future_work: They note that core-set and learning-loss methods, tuned on natural-image benchmarks, capture unlabeled connectomics appearance poorly and that global-average-pooling loss estimators discard object structure. Project page: https://zudi-lin.github.io/projects/#two_stream_active.

summaries.beginner: Experts cannot label every synapse and mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope volume. This paper picks which examples to label next by combining a network trained on labels with another trained on all the raw pictures, and it reports better proposals than earlier active-learning methods.
summaries.intermediate: In ECCV 2020 (Comput Vis ECCV 12363:103–120), Lin and colleagues propose two-stream active query suggestion: a supervised feature extractor plus an unsupervised extractor trained on all raw images and later fine-tuned on new labels. Applied to 3D synapse detection and mitochondria segmentation in connectomics, they report a densely annotated dataset and gains of 3.1% (synapses) and 3.8% (mitochondria) in ROI-proposal accuracy over prior state of the art, plus a CIFAR-10 comparison under a matched annotation budget. An ablation starts from 0.762 instance-proposal accuracy; 4.46% random labels add ~0.01, versus ~0.08 from their clustering with Q = 5 representatives.
summaries.advanced: “Largest” is the authors’ claim, not independently audited here. The 3.1% and 3.8% figures are ROI-proposal accuracy, not final instance segmentation. Ablation numbers are on their synapse benchmark with a fixed annotation budget and cluster count. CIFAR-10 is a natural-image check, not connectomics. Late fusion of streams can be dominated by a 1,000-d image embedding versus a 20-d mask embedding.

plain_language_summary: Experts cannot label every synapse and mitochondrion in a huge electron-microscope volume. This paper picks which examples to label next by combining a network trained on labels with another trained on all the raw pictures, and it reports better proposals than earlier active-learning methods.

ocar.opportunity: The Drosophila larva is small enough that synapse-resolution wiring, cellular-resolution activity, and behavior can in principle be combined for the same circuits.
ocar.challenge: Even with those tools, it is still hard to state which circuit motifs implement multisensory integration, learning, and action selection, and how brain, subesophageal zone, and ventral nerve cord divide those jobs.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2020), Eschbach and Zlatic review recently reconstructed larval CNS circuits, emphasizing first-instar EM, genetic single-cell targeting, and whole-brain imaging.
ocar.resolution: They note an early larval CNS of about 15,000 neurons, with somatosensory and motor circuits in the VNC, feeding and neuromodulation in the SEZ, and first- and higher-order sensory centers in the brain reconstructed in the same EM volume; comprehensive CNS reconstruction is described as within reach. Gerhard et al. are cited for synaptic-input fractions that remain similar despite a five-fold size change from first to third instar. Themes include early multisensory loops for specific actions versus more centralized valence-like signals in higher areas.
ocar.future_work: Open questions include how descending brain/SEZ neurons bias VNC somatosensory choices, and using multi-individual connectomes to study memory traces, individuality, and mutants.

summaries.beginner: The fruit-fly maggot has a small nervous system, so wiring, activity, and behavior can be studied together. This review gathers recent maps of how the larva combines senses, learns, and chooses actions.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2020, 65:129–137), Eschbach and Zlatic review Drosophila larva CNS connectomics. They contrast the early larva’s roughly 15,000 smaller neurons with the adult, and they summarize synaptic-resolution reconstructions in one first-instar EM volume covering VNC somatosensory and motor programs, SEZ feeding and neuromodulation, and brain sensory and associative centers. They highlight Gerhard et al. on conserved synaptic-input fractions despite five-fold growth, and they organize recent results around multisensory integration, mushroom-body learning (including recurrent dopaminergic motifs), and action selection such as crawl-versus-turn.
summaries.advanced: This is a review, not a new reconstruction. Neuron counts, circuit lists, and the five-fold size comparison are cited from other papers. “Comprehensive reconstruction within reach” was a 2020 outlook. Functional claims (valence-like signals, specific sensorimotor loops) synthesize physiology plus anatomy from the cited studies. The tripartite insect/vertebrate analogy is organizational, not a homology proof.

plain_language_summary: The fruit-fly maggot has a small nervous system, so wiring, activity, and behavior can be studied together. This review gathers recent maps of how the larva combines senses, learns, and chooses actions.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomics usually reverse-engineers existing brains, while synthetic biology forward-engineers living systems from parts; combining them could let researchers build and test wiring diagrams in behaving animals.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear what a designed, constructed connectome would look like, what scientific or societal purposes it would serve, and how it could be built.
ocar.action: Rabinowitch, in Physics of Life Reviews (2020), reviews the idea of synthetic connectomics: artificially designing and constructing connectomes of live behaving organisms as a platform to test theories of network function and possibly new forms of artificial life.
ocar.resolution: The article is a conceptual review rather than a constructed organism: it argues that building a system is a powerful way to understand it, sketches purposes (unifying brain-operation questions; exploring theoretical network predictions empirically), and aims to lay initial implementation steps and contemplate scientific and social impact.
ocar.future_work: The review itself is the proposed research program: methods of construction, design goals, and impact remain prospective.

summaries.beginner: Most brain-wiring research takes animals apart; a complementary idea is to design and build wiring on purpose. This review asks what a synthetic connectome would be for and how one might start making one.
summaries.intermediate: In Physics of Life Reviews (2020), Rabinowitch proposes synthetic connectomics as a meeting point of connectomics and synthetic biology: the artificial design and construction of connectomes in live behaving organisms. The piece contrasts reverse-engineering of existing brains with construction-based forward-engineering, and it frames synthetic connectomes as a way to test theoretical predictions about network function and, more speculatively, to generate new forms of artificial life. It is organized around three questions—what such a connectome would look like, what it would be for, and how it could be constructed—and is explicitly a conceptual outline rather than a methods paper with results.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is Perkins, Gandara, and Crocker, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 377:20200517 (2022), “A synthetic synthesis to explore animal evolution and development,” not Rabinowitch. This card uses only the catalog abstract. The article is a perspective/review with no empirical connectome or organism constructed. Claims about unifying platforms and artificial life are programmatic.

plain_language_summary: Most brain-wiring research takes animals apart; a complementary idea is to design and build wiring on purpose. This review asks what a synthetic connectome would be for and how one might start making one.

ocar.opportunity: Animals reuse the same motor neurons for distinct or even antagonistic behaviors, but how timing among those neurons is switched is unclear.
ocar.challenge: Without a complete premotor-to-motor wiring diagram for a segment, labeled-line, combinatorial, morphological, and motif explanations of forward versus backward crawling cannot be compared in one animal.
ocar.action: In eLife (2019), Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe combine larval Drosophila muscle calcium imaging with TEM reconstruction of all 60 motor neurons and 236 premotor neurons in one segment, then fit a recurrent network and test selected predictions with optogenetics.
ocar.resolution: All imaged body-wall motor neurons are active in both forward and backward locomotion, but a subset changes recruitment timing. Connectome analysis finds labeled-line and combinatorial PMN–MN connectivity, asymmetric morphology, and circuit motifs that could support the two behaviors. A recurrent model without post-inhibitory rebound or spike-frequency adaptation reproduced observed motor timing; optogenetics validated selected predictions. All imaged body-wall muscles were bifunctional.
ocar.future_work: The authors present the PMN–MN connectome as a foundation for the rest of the larval motor suite (rolling, righting, turning, digging) and note that intrinsic neuronal dynamics are likely richer than the model.

summaries.beginner: The same larval muscles have to crawl both forward and backward. This study maps every motor neuron and its premotor partners in one body segment, then shows that timing—not a separate muscle set—distinguishes the two gaits.
summaries.intermediate: In eLife (2019), Zarin, Mark, Cardona, Litwin-Kumar, and Doe image Drosophila larval muscle activity and reconstruct one TEM segment containing 60 motor neurons and 236 premotor neurons. All body-wall MNs are recruited in both forward and backward crawling, with a subset changing timing. They describe labeled-line and combinatorial PMN–MN connectivity, asymmetric morphology, and motifs, and they train a recurrent model that reproduces the two motor patterns without complex single-cell dynamics; selected predictions are tested optogenetically. They argue a single recurrent premotor layer can suffice for multiple outputs.
summaries.advanced: Reconstruction is one segment, not the whole larva. The model omits command-like third-layer neurons and intrinsic properties known to matter in other CPGs; the authors say those dynamics are likely present but not required in the fit. Bifunctionality is for imaged body-wall muscles in locomotion, not a census of all larval behaviors. Optogenetic tests cover selected model predictions, not the full motif list.

plain_language_summary: The same larval muscles have to crawl both forward and backward. This study maps every motor neuron and its premotor partners in one body segment, then shows that timing—not a separate muscle set—distinguishes the two gaits.

ocar.opportunity: Electron- and light-sheet volumes are now too large for manual instance segmentation, and convolutional nets still need proofreading because their field of view cannot encode long-range cell-shape priors that humans use.
ocar.challenge: Biological knowledge such as expected morphology or ultrastructure is hard to inject into a local boundary classifier without an explicit long-range partitioning model.
ocar.action: Pape, Matskevych, Wolny, Hennies, Mizzon, Louveaux, Musser, Maizel, Arendt, and Kreshuk (Frontiers in Computer Science / arXiv, 2019) encode domain knowledge as long-range interactions in the lifted multicut graph-partitioning problem.
ocar.resolution: They report improved segmentation accuracy on four challenging boundary-based problems in neuroscience and developmental biology (the catalog abstract says three EM problems). Examples in the extract include resolving false merges in Drosophila medulla and plant-root light-sheet data. Joint lifted-multicut with short-range terms (LMC-S) is more accurate than iterative correction (LMC-SI), consistent with preventing merges being cheaper than fixing them.
ocar.future_work: They point to a combined lifted-edge plus semantic-label objective (Levinkov et al.) for neuron segmentation, and to extra priors such as cell-type matching, manual skeletons, or correlative light microscopy.

summaries.beginner: Automatic cell cutting in microscope images still glues the wrong objects together because the computer only looks at a small neighborhood. This paper turns extra biological knowledge into long-distance “don’t merge these” links and shows cleaner cells in several hard datasets.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Computer Science (2019; arXiv:1905.10535v2), Pape and colleagues cast domain-specific priors as lifted edges in a lifted-multicut partition. The PDF reports significant accuracy gains on four boundary-based instance-segmentation problems in neuroscience and developmental biology, including Drosophila medulla EM (oracle-flagged merge repair) and plant-root membrane/nucleus volumes. They argue that jointly using dense short-range and sparse long-range information beats an iterative resolve-afterward pipeline, matching earlier observations that preventing merges is more efficient than correcting them.
summaries.advanced: The catalog abstract says three EM problems; the PDF says four boundary-based problems including light microscopy—this card follows the PDF. Medulla experiments include an oracle whose F-score is swept from 0.5 to 1, so fully automatic performance depends on the merge detector. Lifted-multicut quality depends on how priors are turned into long-range edges. Results are problem-specific, not a universal EM leaderboard score.

plain_language_summary: Automatic cell cutting in microscope images still glues the wrong objects together because the computer only looks at a small neighborhood. This paper turns extra biological knowledge into long-distance “don’t merge these” links and shows cleaner cells in several hard datasets.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding how C. elegans turns a complete connectome into crawling requires coupling neurons, muscles, body mechanics, and proprioception in one simulatable system, with room to swap biophysical modules.
ocar.challenge: Connectome wiring alone does not specify intracellular dynamics, neuromuscular transformation, or body–environment physics, and isolated CPG stories leave sensorimotor pathways underspecified.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (2019), Kim, Florman, Santos, Alkema, and Shlizerman introduce modWorm: seven exchangeable modules from intracellular and extra-cellular neural dynamics through muscle force to posture and proprioceptive feedback, built on the complete worm connectome.
ocar.resolution: In-silico current injection into locomotion-associated sensory and interneurons, plus external body forces, recapitulates forward and backward crawling and mid-locomotion avoidance and turns. In-silico ablation surveys are used to infer additional sensorimotor circuits. Module variants and parameter optimization are compared with experimental locomotion findings.
ocar.future_work: The authors warn that optimizing connectome parameters on a subset of behaviors can hurt others, and they suggest multi-objective training, deep-learning wrappers, and community use of the GitHub codebase (to be public upon publication).

summaries.beginner: A worm’s wiring diagram does not by itself crawl. This modeling kit chains neurons, muscles, and body physics so simulated pokes and ablations can be compared with real locomotion.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Kim, Florman, Santos, Alkema, and Shlizerman present modWorm, a modular C. elegans neuro-mechanical model on the complete connectome with seven stages: intracellular dynamics; electrical and chemical extra-cellular coupling; neural activity to muscle calcium; calcium to force; force to posture; and proprioceptive feedback. Constant-current injections and body forces reproduce forward/backward locomotion and stimulus-triggered avoidance and turns; ablation surveys propose additional circuits. The framework is intended for swapping empirical dynamics and for parameter searches against experimental locomotion.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint; the extract says code “will be made public upon publication.” Recapitulated behaviors are in-silico under injected currents, not closed-loop experimental replication in this paper. Ablation-inferred circuits are model predictions. Authors note that fitting a subset of behaviors can create inaccuracies in others. Results depend on polarity, muscle, and proprioception module choices.

plain_language_summary: A worm’s wiring diagram does not by itself crawl. This modeling kit chains neurons, muscles, and body physics so simulated pokes and ablations can be compared with real locomotion.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans pharynx is a self-contained neuromuscular organ whose 20 neurons (14 anatomical types) can be rewired in detail as a model of a simple, autonomous nervous system.
ocar.challenge: The classic map classified cells as inter- versus motor neurons and undercounted cross-connectivity, leaving sensory roles and computational modules unclear.
ocar.action: In the Journal of Comparative Neurology (2020), Cook, Crouse, Yemini, Hall, Emmons, and Hobert re-evaluate the pharyngeal connectome with serial-section EM.
ocar.resolution: Most pharyngeal neurons are likely sensory as well as motor, yielding a shallow sensory-motor architecture with more extensive neuron–neuron synapses than previously realized. Connection patterns fall into modules matching corpus, isthmus, and terminal bulb. Relative to the somatic nervous system, pharyngeal neurons physically contact and synapse onto a larger fraction of neighbors. The authors speculate that this architecture may resemble ancestral primitive nervous systems.
ocar.future_work: Mechanisms of the primitive sensors (no true cilium or basal body) remain open, as does linking the few central neurons to the generally weak pumping phenotypes of single-cell ablations.

summaries.beginner: The worm’s throat has its own tiny nervous system of twenty cells. A new electron-microscope map finds that most of those cells both sense and drive muscle, in shallow modules matched to parts of the pharynx.
summaries.intermediate: In J. Comp. Neurol. (2020, 528:2767–2784), Cook and colleagues reconstruct the C. elegans pharyngeal nervous system (20 neurons, 14 types) by serial EM, extending Albertson and Thomson (1976). They argue that most neurons are likely sensory and that most or all are motor, with denser cross-connectivity than previously cataloged, producing a shallow network organized into modules for corpus, isthmus, and terminal bulb. Pharyngeal cells associate and synapse with a larger fraction of neighbors than somatic neurons. Comparative remarks place the map among other small connectomes including P. pacificus pharynx.
summaries.advanced: The catalog lists bioRxiv; the extract is the published JCN article. Sensory function is anatomical inference (endings, not new physiology). “Most if not all are motor neurons” depends on scoring synapses onto end organs. Ancestral-architecture language is speculative. Ablation literature cited as often weak for pumping, so modules are not equivalent to necessary-and-sufficient pumping controllers.

plain_language_summary: The worm’s throat has its own tiny nervous system of twenty cells. A new electron-microscope map finds that most of those cells both sense and drive muscle, in shallow modules matched to parts of the pharynx.

ocar.opportunity: Head-direction-like compass activity is widely modeled as a ring attractor, but the assumed excitatory and inhibitory wiring has been hard to check in a real circuit.
ocar.challenge: Theoretical rings require specific recurrence to hold a bump in darkness, shift it with turns, and tether it to vision; mixed pre- and postsynaptic arbors and split inhibition are not in the textbook diagrams.
ocar.action: In a January 2020 bioRxiv preprint, Turner-Evans, Jensen, Ali, Paterson, Sheridan, Ray, Wolff, Lauritzen, Rubin, Bock, and Jayaraman combine EM reconstruction and RNA profiling of Drosophila heading-direction cell types with two-photon imaging and thermogenetic perturbation during behavior.
ocar.resolution: They identify hypothesized motifs: E-PG neurons construct the heading representation; P-EN1 supply angular-velocity update; Δ7 provide inhibition that sculpts P-EN1; visual ring neurons contact E-PGs. Extrapolated synapse-count matrices resemble a previously tuned ring-attractor model. They also find unpredicted recurrence between mixed pre/post arbors, inhibition split across Δ7 and multiple GABAergic ring populations (E-PG bumps persist when Δ7 output is reduced), and local excitation via several classes.
ocar.future_work: Further theory is needed for split inhibition, mixed-polarity arbors, and how a small neuron count still tracks heading smoothly; Gall-EB ring neurons were not reconstructed but FISH supports that they are GABAergic.

summaries.beginner: Flies keep an internal compass of which way their head points, and theories say that takes a ring of cells that excite neighbors and inhibit opposites. This team checks the actual synapses and finds the predicted parts plus extra loops the models did not include.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint posted 19 January 2020, Turner-Evans and colleagues reconstruct the Drosophila heading network with EM, profile cell-type RNA, and combine two-photon imaging with thermogenetic perturbation. They map E-PG, P-EN1, Δ7, and ring-neuron motifs onto ring-attractor roles (hold in darkness, update on turns, tether to visual cues) and report that a connectivity matrix built from synapse counts resembles a previously weight-tuned model. Unpredicted features include mixed pre- and postsynaptic specializations, inhibition distributed across Δ7 and visual/Gall-EB ring neurons, and local excitation among E-PGs and P-ENs in both ellipsoid body and protocerebral bridge.
summaries.advanced: This extract is a preprint. Functional support is additional imaging/perturbation, not a full causal dissection of every motif. Extrapolating local synapse counts around the ring assumes rotational completeness. Δ7 is not sufficient as the sole inhibitory source. Gap-junction and neuromodulatory contributions are outside the chemical-synapse reconstruction. Compass dynamics in a few dozen neurons may rely on the extra recurrence the authors flag as unexplained by simple rings.

plain_language_summary: Flies keep an internal compass of which way their head points, and theories say that takes a ring of cells that excite neighbors and inhibit opposites. This team checks the actual synapses and finds the predicted parts plus extra loops the models did not include.

ocar.opportunity: Female Drosophila avoid the mold odor geosmin when choosing where to lay eggs, a stereotyped valence that can be traced from receptors through the brain to descending output.
ocar.challenge: Whether that pathway stays a labeled line or becomes a distributed central representation, and where it converges with other aversive odors such as parasitoid-wasp pheromone, is not visible from the first synapse alone.
ocar.action: Huoviala, Dolan, Love, Myers, Frechter, Namiki, Pettersson, Roberts, Turnbull, Mitrevica, Breads, Schlegel, Bates, Rodrigues, Aso, Bock, Rubin, Stensmyr, Card, Costa, and Jefferis (bioRxiv, 2020 version) combine genetics, physiology, behavior, and FAFB connectomics.
ocar.resolution: Avoidance in a two-choice egg-laying assay is olfactory and Or56a-dependent; geosmin does not reduce egg number in a no-choice setting. Or56a ORNs synapse on uniglomerular DA2 projection neurons that remain geosmin-selective (labeled line at the second order). Those PNs contact a diverse set of 80 third-order cell types, with valence-specific convergence including axo-axonic input onto second-order neurons of another danger cue (wasp pheromone). Descending neurons required for egg-laying aversion sit one more synapse downstream.
ocar.future_work: FAFB reconstructions were to be shared with Virtual Fly Brain upon publication. The proposed picture is a transition from peripheral labeled lines to a distributed central representation coupled to distinct descending pathways.

summaries.beginner: Female fruit flies refuse to lay eggs where they smell a mold chemical. This study follows that smell from the antenna through many brain cells to the neurons that send the “don’t lay here” command, and it finds both a private line and a lot of mixing with other bad smells.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (doi 10.1101/394403; version posted 4 November 2020), Huoviala, Jefferis, and colleagues trace geosmin egg-laying aversion from Or56a sensory neurons onto cholinergic DA2 projection neurons, which remain highly geosmin-selective, then onto about 80 third-order types, then to descending neurons needed for the aversion. They report valence-specific convergence, including axo-axonic input onto second-order neurons that carry parasitoid-wasp pheromone, alongside broad divergence in the lateral horn. Behaviorally, two-choice positional avoidance is olfactory and Or56a-dependent, whereas no-choice egg counts do not fall.
summaries.advanced: No journal venue is set in the catalog; this is a preprint. “Complete synaptic circuit from sensory input to descending output” is a connectomic plus functional composite, not every synapse in every animal. Third-order diversity (80 types) makes labeled-line language inappropriate past the PN layer. Axo-axonic “danger” convergence is structural plus the authors’ valence assignment. Descending-neuron necessity is from the functional screen described, not from the EM volume alone.

plain_language_summary: Female fruit flies refuse to lay eggs where they smell a mold chemical. This study follows that smell from the antenna through many brain cells to the neurons that send the “don’t lay here” command, and it finds both a private line and a lot of mixing with other bad smells.

ocar.opportunity: Recovering an insect wiring diagram requires not only neuron segmentation but identification of synaptic partners, and fly synapses are polyadic: one presynaptic site faces several postsynaptic partners.
ocar.challenge: Voxel-level cleft or vesicle labels are expensive, and partner identity is a long-range relation that standard local synapse detectors do not encode.
ocar.action: In MICCAI (2018), Buhmann, Krause, Ceballos Lentini, Eckstein, Cook, Turaga, and Funke train a 3D U-Net to classify long-range edges between voxels as directed synaptic pairs, learning from point annotations.
ocar.resolution: On the MICCAI 2016 CREMI challenge they report 3% fewer errors than the previous leader (about 19% fewer total false positives plus false negatives; test f-score 0.55 versus a 3% f-score gain; validation f-score 0.75). They note some apparent false positives are likely missed ground-truth synapses. Predicted connectivity matrices resemble ground truth despite modest precision/recall (0.78/0.73 on validation).
ocar.future_work: They propose replacing discrete long-range edges with a continuous regression of postsynaptic offset, and they flag failures on very small postsynaptic profiles and synapses in the cutting plane.

summaries.beginner: In a fly brain, one sending site often talks to several receiving sites, so finding “who synapses with whom” is harder than circling a dark blob. This method learns those pairs from simple point clicks and led a public challenge at the time.
summaries.intermediate: In MICCAI 2018, Buhmann and colleagues formulate synaptic-partner prediction as classification of directed long-range voxel edges in a 3D U-Net, trained from point annotations rather than dense cleft masks, targeting polyadic Drosophila synapses. Evaluated on CREMI (MICCAI 2016) with an automated neuron segmentation from a prior U-Net paper, they report a 3% f-score gain over the previous leader and describe that as about 19% fewer combined false positives and negatives; the discussion states an overall test f-score of 0.55. Validation f-score is 0.75 with precision 0.78 and recall 0.73. Context per voxel is 212×212×28 voxels (848×848×1120 nm).
summaries.advanced: Test-set f-score 0.55 shows the task remained hard. The 3% versus 19% discrepancy is explained in-text by equal averaging of samples with different synapse counts. Some “errors” are blamed on incomplete ground truth. Partner extraction uses a separate automated segmentation, so neuron-split errors propagate. The discretized long-range-edge representation may not match synapse geometry elsewhere in the volume.

plain_language_summary: In a fly brain, one sending site often talks to several receiving sites, so finding “who synapses with whom” is harder than circling a dark blob. This method learns those pairs from simple point clicks and led a public challenge at the time.

ocar.opportunity: The C. elegans connectome has been known for decades, but locomotion models still lack signs (excitation versus inhibition) on the synapses of the small pre-motor circuit.
ocar.challenge: Even seven neurons generate a huge space of polarity patterns, and the same anatomy can produce many dynamics depending on signs, modulation, and input.
ocar.action: In PLoS Computational Biology (2017), Rakowski and Karbowski combine genetic algorithms, large-scale parallel search, and conductance-level interneuron models, scoring polarity patterns against published locomotory ablation data.
ocar.resolution: The polarity pattern that best matches the locomotory data is all-inhibitory among pre-motor interneurons, including connections onto motor neurons, for links that are not too weak. They interpret this as consistent with cholinergic signaling data and as a metabolic-energy-saving design, and they offer the search method for other small worm circuits.
ocar.future_work: They acknowledge that some of the weakest connections (examples include AVA to AVD, AVA to AVE, PVC to AVE) might still be excitatory. Uncertain biophysical parameters are outputs of the same global fit, not independent measurements.

summaries.beginner: Knowing who is wired to whom in a worm does not say whether each wire pushes or brakes. A computer search over a seven-cell locomotion circuit finds that the best match to crawling data is inhibition on essentially every connection.
summaries.intermediate: In PLoS Computational Biology (2017), Rakowski and Karbowski infer synaptic polarities in a seven-neuron C. elegans pre-motor locomotion circuit by pairing detailed interneuron dynamics with a genetic-algorithm search scored against behavioral data (including ablation conditions). The optimal pattern matching those data is exclusive inhibition among interneurons, including terminals onto motor neurons, when connections are not too weak. They relate this to cholinergic signaling results and to an energy-saving interpretation (stationary current balances are shown across ablation conditions). Code is pointed to GitHub (elegans-simulation / evolutionary-algorithm / elegans-optimisation).
summaries.advanced: Polarities are reverse-engineered from behavior plus a specific biophysical model, not measured at each synapse. “All inhibitory” applies to the pre-motor circuit under their similarity function, with an explicit caveat for the weakest links. Parameter values emerge from the same optimization, so they are not independent validation. Energy saving is an interpretation of inhibitory design, not a calorimetry result.

plain_language_summary: Knowing who is wired to whom in a worm does not say whether each wire pushes or brakes. A computer search over a seven-cell locomotion circuit finds that the best match to crawling data is inhibition on essentially every connection.

ocar.opportunity: Connectomic reconstruction from serial-section EM depends on detecting neuronal boundaries in highly anisotropic image stacks.
ocar.challenge: Section thickness and alignment errors make the z axis much worse than xy, so 2D max-pooling convnets had become the default even though they underuse 3D context.
ocar.action: At NeurIPS (2015), Lee, Zlateski, Vishwanathan, and Seung train a much deeper hybrid 2D–3D convolutional net, recursively feeding a first network’s boundary map into a second net, with back-propagation implemented in ZNN on multicore CPUs.
ocar.resolution: They report a substantial accuracy gain from depth, 3D filters, and recursion. They interpret the recursive map as a task-specific gate that suppresses mitochondria and other distractors, visible as cleaner oriented-boundary feature maps. They note the architecture could extend to 3D affinity graphs by replacing softmax with three affinity outputs, and that ZNN’s dense output patches enable topological losses such as MALIS.
ocar.future_work: The immediate product is improved 2D boundary maps for a 2D-then-3D reconstruction pipeline; direct 3D affinities and topological training objectives are proposed extensions.

summaries.beginner: Serial-section electron-microscope stacks are sharp in the plane of the slice and fuzzy between slices, which makes cell outlines hard for computers. This paper uses a deeper 3D-aware network twice—once for a draft outline, then again to clean it—and reports a clear accuracy jump.
summaries.intermediate: In Neural Information Processing Systems (2015; arXiv:1508.04843), Lee, Zlateski, Vishwanathan, and Seung target neuronal boundary detection in anisotropic serial-section EM. Three changes relative to 2D max-pooling convnets are a much deeper net, mixed 2D and 3D filters, and recursive training in which a second net sees the raw image plus a preliminary boundary map. Training uses ZNN, a CPU-parallel 3D convnet implementation. They argue recursion acts as top-down modulation that preserves boundary signal and suppresses distractors, and they discuss extending the net to x/y/z affinity graphs.
summaries.advanced: The extract does not report a numeric test-set score; “substantial gain” is the authors’ summary. The method is optimized for 2D boundaries as input to a later 3D pipeline, not end-to-end instance segmentation. Recursive stages are trained sequentially, not as a single unrolled objective in the description here. Serial-section artifacts (thickness, alignment) remain in the data. ZNN versus GPU frameworks is a 2015 engineering claim.

plain_language_summary: Serial-section electron-microscope stacks are sharp in the plane of the slice and fuzzy between slices, which makes cell outlines hard for computers. This paper uses a deeper 3D-aware network twice—once for a draft outline, then again to clean it—and reports a clear accuracy jump.

ocar.opportunity: Mammalian brains mix modular, cheap local wiring with expensive integrative hubs, but MRI connectomes are indirect; mouse tract tracing can test whether wiring-cost minimization alone explains the graph.
ocar.challenge: If hubs exist only to shorten paths, they should be explained by a cost-minimizing embedding; if they exist for integration, they should be spatially expensive and linked to cognitive gene expression.
ocar.action: In PNAS (2015), Rubinov, Ypma, Watson, and Bullmore analyze 461 systematically acquired anterograde-tracer injections into right cortical and subcortical mouse regions, estimating weights, distances, and wiring costs of a weighted directed regional connectome.
ocar.resolution: The mouse connectome is small-world, hierarchically modular, and more expensive than a wiring-minimizing null. High-participation hubs mediate communication between specialized, localized modules, have especially high wiring cost, correspond closely to default-mode-network regions, and colocalize with low neuronal density and high expression of genes enriched for cognition, learning and memory, and behavior.
ocar.future_work: The authors propose simultaneous selection for cost minimization and hub-mediated integration as the evolutionary account; the analysis is regional tract tracing, not synapse-level EM.

summaries.beginner: Brains might save wire by keeping connections short, but some regions still make costly long-distance links. In the mouse, those expensive hubs sit where modules meet and line up with genes used in learning and memory.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2015), Rubinov, Ypma, Watson, and Bullmore build a weighted, directed mouse brain connectome from 461 anterograde-tracer injections into right-hemisphere cortical and subcortical regions. Multiscale graph and spatial analyses show small-world structure, hierarchical modularity, and greater-than-minimal wiring cost. High-participation hubs are expensive, match default-mode-network territories, and, in independent histology and Allen gene-expression data, coincide with low neuronal density and transcripts enriched for cognition, learning/memory, and behavior. They frame this as a trade-off between Ramón y Cajal-style cost and topological integration.
summaries.advanced: This is a regional tract-tracing connectome (injections into the right hemisphere), not a synaptic EM map; weak projections and injection coverage bias weights. “Default mode” correspondence is anatomical overlap, not resting-state fMRI in the same mice. Gene-expression associations are spatial correlations, not causal. Wiring-cost nulls depend on how distance and weight are estimated. Hub participation is a graph statistic, not a measured information-flow rate.

plain_language_summary: Brains might save wire by keeping connections short, but some regions still make costly long-distance links. In the mouse, those expensive hubs sit where modules meet and line up with genes used in learning and memory.

ocar.opportunity: Even very low error rates in pixel-wise boundary prediction still break connectomic reconstruction, so architectures closer to human labeling remain valuable.
ocar.challenge: Standard multilayer convnets were, at the time, narrow, short-range, expensive to train, and did not explicitly reuse label-space structure across recursive passes.
ocar.action: Huang and Jain (arXiv/ICLR 2013) introduce Deep And Wide Multiscale Recursive (DAWMR) networks: thousands of features, a large field of view, recursive iterations, a parallelizable training scheme, and a boundary-specific example-weighting rule, tested on 3D EM connectomics.
ocar.resolution: The highest-performing architecture has twelve layers with interleaved supervised and unsupervised stages and a 54³ (157,464-voxel) field of view per prediction. They report new levels of image-labeling performance on neural-circuit EM and release open-source software for building DAWMR nets. Recursion is trained stage-wise rather than end-to-end to cut training time and to allow non-differentiable intermediate features.
ocar.future_work: They suggest feeding object-level geometric features from intermediate segmentations into later iterations, as an alternative to superpixels for fixing undersegmentation. Acknowledgments mention FIB-SEM imaging.

summaries.beginner: Computers that paint every pixel as “cell edge or not” still make enough mistakes to wreck a wiring diagram. This 2013 network looks at a large 3D neighborhood, uses thousands of features, and refines its own labels in extra passes.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2013 arXiv preprint associated with ICLR, Huang and Jain describe DAWMR networks for dense image labeling, emphasizing width (thousands of features), a large field of view, recursive use of prior labels, and faster-to-train parallel stages versus then-standard convnets. For EM boundary prediction they add an example-weighting scheme. The best architecture has twelve layers, mixed supervised/unsupervised stages, and a 54³ = 157,464-voxel input window. They release accompanying open-source software. Recursive iterations are not back-propagated end-to-end, by design.
summaries.advanced: No numeric Rand-index values from the extract are used here because the figure text is not a reliable source of exact scores. Comparisons to convolutional-network baselines are qualitative in this card. Stage-wise recursion may underperform true end-to-end training. “New levels of performance” is the authors’ 2013 claim on their EM set. Catalog venue is ICLR; the extract is the arXiv v3 PDF.

plain_language_summary: Computers that paint every pixel as “cell edge or not” still make enough mistakes to wreck a wiring diagram. This 2013 network looks at a large 3D neighborhood, uses thousands of features, and refines its own labels in extra passes.

ocar.opportunity: Vertebrate vision depends on knowing a complete synaptic graph of at least one retina, but even well-studied cell types have not had their full subnetworks mapped.
ocar.challenge: Graph theory implies that physiology and modeling cannot uniquely invert a multi-edge digraph of this complexity: the human retina has about 70 cell classes, and motif finding is computationally intractable.
ocar.action: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012), Marc, Jones, Lauritzen, Watt, and Anderson review how to build retinal connectomes: TEM at 2 nm or better, molecular tags for cell identity, open volumes, and open-source annotation.
ocar.resolution: They argue TEM is optimal for marking chemical synapses and gap junctions; molecular or optical tags are required to pre-select types; and existing EM platforms can be converted rather than only artisanal tools. Early retinal connectomics already shows richer graphs than expected for nominally known cells.
ocar.future_work: They call for more shared platforms, commercial high-resolution systems analogous to fMRI, comparative connectomics of development and evolution, and pathoconnectomics of retinal neurodegeneration.

summaries.beginner: You cannot guess a retina’s full wiring from recordings alone—there are too many possible graphs. This review says complete maps need very high-resolution electron microscopy plus molecular tags, and that even “known” cells are turning out more connected than textbooks suggested.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2012, 22:568–574), Marc and colleagues argue that retinal and brain networks are multi-edge digraphs whose inverse problems are underdetermined (even a 3-vertex labeled digraph admits 64 networks; human retina about 70 classes). They recommend transmission EM at 2 nm or better, ultrastructurally compliant molecular tags, open-access volumes, and shared or converted commercial TEM platforms. Highlights state that complete retinal networks must be mapped, not inferred, and that first connectomic forays reveal unexpected complexity in well-studied neurons.
summaries.advanced: This is a 2012 opinion/review, not a released complete retinal connectome. The 2 nm TEM preference is the authors’ methodological stance versus other EM platforms then in use. Cell-class counts are cited estimates. “Richer connection graphs than expected” summarizes early annotations, not a quantitative census in this paper. Publisher’s PDF is an unedited accepted manuscript.

plain_language_summary: You cannot guess a retina’s full wiring from recordings alone—there are too many possible graphs. This review says complete maps need very high-resolution electron microscopy plus molecular tags, and that even “known” cells are turning out more connected than textbooks suggested.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome reconstruction from large EM collections requires automated neuron segmentation, which starts with finding membranes amid noise, anisotropy, and confounding organelles.
ocar.challenge: A single classifier that sees only local intensity struggles with gaps and look-alike dark structures; methods that do not learn filters from data also burden users.
ocar.action: In Medical Image Analysis (2010), Jurrus, Paiva, Watanabe, Anderson, Jones, Whitaker, Jorgensen, Marc, and Tasdizen apply a series of artificial neural networks whose features are image intensities on a stencil neighborhood, each net using the previous net’s classification as context.
ocar.resolution: Serial (auto-context) ANNs improve membrane detection over a traditional ANN and over prior membrane detectors. On the Weizmann Horse dataset, used to compare with Tu’s method, they report an f-value of 0.834 versus 0.84, with negligible qualitative difference, while learning filters from data. They show flood-fill segmentations from detected membranes without manual correction as a step toward 3D models.
ocar.future_work: Given anisotropic serial-section TEM, they advocate 2D section segmentation then 3D linking, gap closing, and using adjacent sections; they suggest similar classifiers for tubular MRI vasculature.

summaries.beginner: Cell outlines in electron-microscope pictures are easy for people and hard for computers because of noise and look-alike dark blobs. This 2010 method stacks several small neural nets so each one can use the last one’s guess as extra context.
summaries.intermediate: In Medical Image Analysis (2010, 14:770–783), Jurrus and colleagues detect neuron membranes with serial ANNs: stencil-sampled intensities plus auto-context from the previous network’s output. They report improved detection relative to single ANNs and prior membrane methods. A comparison on Weizmann Horses yields f-value 0.834 versus Tu’s 0.84. They motivate 2D-then-3D linking because of anisotropic TEM, and they illustrate uncorrected flood-fill segmentations. They note that some competing auto-context systems do not scale to a 16 TB rabbit-retina volume.
summaries.advanced: Horse-dataset parity with Tu is not an EM leaderboard win; it is a cross-domain sanity check. Flood-fill figures are qualitative. Serial ANNs still operate per 2D section. Stencil features are not modern deep convnets. User correction is expected to remain for 3D reconstruction. The extract is an NIH author manuscript.

plain_language_summary: Cell outlines in electron-microscope pictures are easy for people and hard for computers because of noise and look-alike dark blobs. This 2010 method stacks several small neural nets so each one can use the last one’s guess as extra context.

ocar.opportunity: Nanoscale connectomics is still too slow to map entire mammalian brains; expansion microscopy raises resolution but cubes the volume, while X-ray tomography could image large volumes quickly if expanded tissue had usable contrast.
ocar.challenge: Apparently no group had imaged cellular features inside expanded tissue with X-ray microscopy, so it was unknown whether contrast sufficient even for cell bodies could be achieved.
ocar.action: Collins (2026) reports an early-stage combination of a modified enzymatic Unclearing protocol with metallic gold stain, imaged on a laboratory X-ray microscope.
ocar.resolution: The paper presents what it describes as the first X-ray reconstruction of cell bodies within expanded tissue. The current iteration resolves cell bodies but not neurites, attributed to extensive off-target staining. The author emphasizes that substantial work remains before “expansion X-ray microscopy” (ExXRM) is useful for connectomics, including adaptation to faster synchrotron X-ray microscopy.
ocar.future_work: Reducing off-target stain to reveal neurites and rewriting the protocol for synchrotron sources are stated as the next requirements.

summaries.beginner: Expanding tissue makes tiny neural details larger, but then there is much more volume to photograph. This early report shows cell bodies in expanded tissue under an X-ray microscope, while still missing the thin wires needed for a wiring diagram.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2026 report, Collins argues that expansion microscopy (ExM) linearly improves resolution but cubically increases imaging time, while X-ray microscopy could accelerate large-volume connectomics if expanded samples had contrast. Combining modified enzymatic Unclearing with a metallic gold stain on a laboratory X-ray microscope, the author reports reconstructions of cell bodies in expanded tissue and introduces the name expansion X-ray microscopy (ExXRM). The present method does not resolve neurites because of off-target staining, and it is not yet adapted to synchrotron X-ray microscopy.
summaries.advanced: PDF extract mismatch: the file is Xu, Gao, Sun, and Wu, “HyperNetWalk,” a cancer-driver-gene method on layered signaling–regulatory networks, not Collins. This card uses only the catalog abstract. There is no journal or DOI in the catalog. “First demonstration” is the author’s claim. ExXRM here is cell-body contrast only, explicitly not connectomic neurite mapping. No quantitative resolution or expansion factor is given in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Expanding tissue makes tiny neural details larger, but then there is much more volume to photograph. This early report shows cell bodies in expanded tissue under an X-ray microscope, while still missing the thin wires needed for a wiring diagram.

ocar.opportunity: Most C. elegans neurons come in left–right pairs, so the connectome is a natural place to ask how bilateral redundancy can coexist with incomplete connection symmetry.
ocar.challenge: Paired cells differ substantially in individual synapses; it is unclear whether they still occupy similar network roles, and whether symmetry of shared edges is enough to explain that similarity.
ocar.action: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2026), Kim, Song, Kralik, and Jeong measure connectivity similarity, motif-fingerprint difference, and path compensation on adult hermaphrodite and male connectomes, with nulls that randomize asymmetric edges while holding symmetric ones.
ocar.resolution: Bilateral pairs show elevated redundancy versus other pairs. Randomizing asymmetric edges while keeping symmetric ones reduces bilateral connectivity similarity, implying that asymmetry itself helps pairs share neighbors and converge on roles. About two-thirds of neurons are paired (198/302 hermaphrodite; 250/385 male). Redundancy is stronger among hermaphrodite interneurons than sensory neurons on all three measures; in the male the gradient is significant only for path compensation.
ocar.future_work: The authors present bilateral redundancy as a multiscale principle not reducible to symmetry. Analyses use published Wormwiring connectomes and public code; no new animals were imaged.

summaries.beginner: Worm neurons often come in left and right twins that are not wired identically. This paper shows those twins still play similar network roles, and that the unmatched wires are part of how they stay similar.
summaries.intermediate: In the European Journal of Neuroscience (2026), Kim, Song, Kralik, and Jeong quantify bilateral redundancy in adult hermaphrodite and male C. elegans connectomes with connectivity similarity (shared in/out-neighbors), motif-fingerprint difference, and a path-compensation index. Bilateral pairs are more redundant than other pairs. A null that shuffles asymmetric edges while freezing symmetric ones lowers connectivity similarity, so residual asymmetry is interpreted as enabling shared neighbors. Pairing rates are 198/302 (hermaphrodite) and 250/385 (male). Interneurons show more redundancy than sensory neurons in the hermaphrodite across all three measures.
summaries.advanced: Measures are graph-theoretic on published chemical/electrical wiring, not functional imaging. “Redundancy” is neighbor/motif/path overlap, not proven degeneracy in behavior. Male versus hermaphrodite differences may mix true sex differences with connectome-reconstruction differences. Null models preserve chosen symmetric edges by construction. Code/data pointers include Wormwiring and a GitHub snapshot.

plain_language_summary: Worm neurons often come in left and right twins that are not wired identically. This paper shows those twins still play similar network roles, and that the unmatched wires are part of how they stay similar.

ocar.opportunity: Essential behaviors such as grooming require coordinating several body parts, but the neural basis of that coordination in a compact brain is incomplete.
ocar.challenge: Antennal grooming synchronizes head, antennae, and forelegs; it is unclear whether that coupling needs proprioception from each appendage or can be explained by centralized brain circuitry.
ocar.action: In Nature Communications (2026, article in press), Özdil, Arreguit, Scherrer, Hurtak, Ijspeert, and Ramdya combine 3D kinematics, a biomechanical model, a brain-connectome antennal-grooming network, a simulated activation screen, and experimental perturbation of broadcast inhibitory neurons.
ocar.resolution: Unilateral and bilateral grooming arise from synchronized head, antennal, and foreleg movements; replaying kinematics in a biomechanical model suggests coordination yields unobstructed, forceful tibia–antenna collisions. Movements of one part do not require proprioceptive feedback from the others: foreleg or antennal amputation or head immobilization does not stop the remaining parts. Connectome analysis highlights centralized interneurons and shared premotor neurons; the activation screen implicates recurrent excitation plus broadcast inhibition, with experimental support from manipulating “asteroid” inhibitory neurons.
ocar.future_work: The authors suggest similarly centralized controllers as a general motif for co-recruiting body parts. The extract is an unedited in-press version.

summaries.beginner: When a fly grooms an antenna, its head, feelers, and front legs move together. This study argues that a central brain circuit, not feedback from each limb, keeps those parts in sync, and that turning off a class of widely broadcasting inhibitory cells disrupts the coordination.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2026, doi 10.1038/s41467-026-72152-x, accepted 7 April 2026), Özdil, Ramdya, and colleagues study Drosophila antennal grooming. Kinematics of unilateral versus bilateral grooming show synchronized head, antenna, and foreleg motion; a biomechanical replay is used to argue for efficient tibia–antenna contact. Appendage amputation and head immobilization indicate that remaining parts still move. A connectome-derived network plus a simulated activation screen points to centralized interneurons, shared premotor neurons, recurrent excitation, and broadcast inhibition; asteroid inhibitory neurons are manipulated experimentally.
summaries.advanced: The PDF is an unedited article-in-press. Biomechanical “efficiency” is a simulation inference. Negative proprioception results show movements can persist without those sensors, not that sensors never contribute in intact flies. Connectome motifs are from a reconstructed network, and the activation screen is simulated. Asteroid-neuron experiments validate one inhibitory class, not the entire controller.

plain_language_summary: When a fly grooms an antenna, its head, feelers, and front legs move together. This study argues that a central brain circuit, not feedback from each limb, keeps those parts in sync, and that turning off a class of widely broadcasting inhibitory cells disrupts the coordination.

ocar.opportunity: Automated EM segmentation makes large connectomes possible, but proofreading is now the dominant cost, and labs lack a ground-truth-free rule for when to stop editing.
ocar.challenge: Most reconstruction-quality metrics need painstaking manual ground truth on subvolumes, which does not scale to deciding a global “pencils down” point.
ocar.action: In a July 2026 bioRxiv preprint, Martinez, Matelsky, Xenes, Merfeld, Cavanaugh, Rivlin, Smith, and Wester track simple global graph invariants as proofreading edits accumulate, using a zebrafish spinal cord and the Drosophila hemibrain.
ocar.resolution: Invariants (including degree Gini, number of components, average degree, component-size and degree coefficients of variation, giant-component fraction, reciprocity, and top 1% degree mass) are described as converging toward asymptotic limits, supplying a quantitative stopping criterion. Background text notes that one cited hemibrain-scale effort took 2.5 person-years to proofread about 5,500 undersegmented cells at about 43 minutes per split edit. The method is intended for budgeting remaining work without a priori ground truth.
ocar.future_work: The approach estimates global graph maturity, not local biological accuracy of every neuron; owners still match stopping points to their scientific questions.

summaries.beginner: Fixing computer mistakes in a huge brain map can consume years, and it is hard to know when the map is “good enough.” This preprint watches a few whole-network statistics as edits roll in and argues they level off at a sensible stopping point.
summaries.intermediate: Posted on bioRxiv 4 July 2026, Martinez and colleagues propose monitoring global graph invariants during connectomic proofreading as a cheap, ground-truth-free progress meter. They illustrate the idea on a zebrafish spinal cord and the Drosophila hemibrain, which sit at different proofreading stages. Table 2 lists expected directions of change (e.g., giant-component fraction up as fragments join; degree Gini as artificial hubs are corrected). They cite a prior effort of 2.5 person-years, about 5,500 undersegmented cells, and about 43 minutes per split, to motivate why a stopping rule matters.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint. Convergence of global invariants does not certify synapse-level correctness or absence of remaining local splits/merges. Some background effort statistics are cited from other hemibrain papers, not newly measured here. Zebrafish spinal cord and fly hemibrain differ in scale and error mix, so fitted asymptotes are dataset-specific. “Optimal” stopping still depends on the downstream scientific question.

plain_language_summary: Fixing computer mistakes in a huge brain map can consume years, and it is hard to know when the map is “good enough.” This preprint watches a few whole-network statistics as edits roll in and argues they level off at a sensible stopping point.

ocar.opportunity: Drosophila flight is a classic model of visual control, and genetic targeting plus a complete connectome now let individual neurons be placed in that control hierarchy.
ocar.challenge: Flight ranges from fast stabilizing reflexes to longer goal-directed maneuvers, so it is unclear how a brain of about 140,000 neurons flexibly gates and recruits those modules.
ocar.action: In Trends in Neurosciences (February 2026), Schnell reviews how visual information is transformed into flight output, from optomotor stabilization to central-complex goal-directed behavior.
ocar.resolution: The review argues for a hierarchy: optomotor responses as reflex-like course stabilization that can be disabled during voluntary turns; central-complex circuits necessary for goal-directed behavior that may recruit saccade generators; direct optic-lobe-to-descending-neuron paths that central circuits can modulate. Flexibility comes from efference copies, behavioral-state-dependent activity, and plasticity, plus a flight-associated brain state involving neuromodulation (including decreased insulin-producing-cell activity cited as preparing for energy use).
ocar.future_work: Outstanding questions concern how hierarchical levels interact to control flight; the piece is a synthesis, not a new circuit map.

summaries.beginner: Fruit flies steer in midair with a relatively small brain. This review says they do it by stacking fast stabilizing reflexes under more flexible, goal-seeking circuits, and by changing how vision is processed depending on whether they are flying.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (February 2026, 49(2)), Schnell reviews visually guided Drosophila flight in the era of cell-type genetics and the whole-brain connectome. The fly brain is given as about 140,000 neurons. Organization is hierarchical: optomotor stabilization, rapid turns, and central-complex goal-directed behavior, with coordinated head, body, and retinal movements shaping visual input. The author emphasizes flexible processing via efference copies, state-dependent gain, and plasticity, and notes that flight accompanies a broader brain/metabolic state. Direct projection-neuron-to-descending-neuron connectivity is described as common but centrally modulable.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of others’ experiments and connectomes. The 140,000-neuron figure is cited from the complete adult fly brain literature. Hierarchical and “comparatively small number of neurons” claims are interpretive. Insulin-producing-cell metabolism is cited from another study. Knowledge gaps about inter-level interaction are acknowledged by the author.

plain_language_summary: Fruit flies steer in midair with a relatively small brain. This review says they do it by stacking fast stabilizing reflexes under more flexible, goal-seeking circuits, and by changing how vision is processed depending on whether they are flying.

ocar.opportunity: Single-neuron connectomes from widely diverged species share clustering, short paths, and heavy-tailed weights and degrees, suggesting developmental rules that do not require activity-dependent fine-tuning.
ocar.challenge: Distance-dependent wiring alone yields small-world graphs but not heavy tails, so additional geometric attachment rules are needed and must be tested at neuron versus area scale.
ocar.action: Morales-Gregorio, Kurth, and Korvasová (arXiv:2601.05021, 2026) analyze neuron-resolution connectomes from C. elegans, Platynereis, Drosophila, zebrafish, and mouse, and compare generative models with distance dependence (D), plus weight-preferential (W) and degree-preferential (K) attachment.
ocar.resolution: D produces small-world structure without heavy tails; D+W matches heavy-tailed weights; adding K matches heavy-tailed degrees. The combination is reported as sufficient for characteristic empirical properties. The same model does not generalize to area-level tract-tracing graphs (mouse, marmoset, macaque), which are denser, less degree-heavy-tailed, and fit best with β = 0 (no degree-preferential attachment), consistent with undersampling of weak long-range projections.
ocar.future_work: The authors interpret the neuron-scale trio as activity-independent geometric constraints that could be universal for circuit assembly; area-scale networks appear to need different principles.

summaries.beginner: Brains from worms to mice look alike in some wiring statistics, as if development followed simple geometric rules. This study shows that how far cells are apart, plus two “rich-get-richer” rules for synapses and branches, can recreate those statistics—unless you zoom out to whole brain areas.
summaries.intermediate: In a January 2026 arXiv preprint, Morales-Gregorio, Kurth, and Korvasová compare single-neuron connectomes of C. elegans, Platynereis, Drosophila, zebrafish, and mouse.
