Distance-dependent connectivity (D) yields small-world graphs but not heavy-tailed weights or degrees; adding weight-preferential attachment from synaptic clustering (W) and degree-preferential attachment from arbor extent (K) reproduces those tails. Parameter scans support D+W+K as sufficient at neuron resolution. Area-level tract-tracing connectomes (e.g., marmoset N = 55, density 0.624) are not well captured; D+W+K prefers β = 0, and sampling bias against weak connections is discussed.
summaries.advanced: No journal venue or DOI in the catalog. “Sufficient” means matching selected statistics of empirical graphs, not proving uniqueness of the developmental mechanism. Activity-independence is an interpretation of the generative ingredients, not a developmental experiment. Tract-tracing area networks are collated across animals and undersample weak connections by the authors’ own caveat. Homophily is discussed as an alternative constraint not required in their successful neuron-scale mix.

plain_language_summary: Brains from worms to mice look alike in some wiring statistics, as if development followed simple geometric rules. This study shows that how far cells are apart, plus two “rich-get-richer” rules for synapses and branches, can recreate those statistics—unless you zoom out to whole brain areas.

ocar.opportunity: MICrONS provides the same mouse visual-cortical neurons with EM wiring, spatial coordinates, and calcium imaging, a rare chance to use cortex as an inductive bias for recurrent nets.
ocar.challenge: It is unclear which of geometry, anatomical connectivity, and functional relationships actually help RNNs learn, and whether the resulting networks adopt brain-like modular small-world structure.
ocar.action: In an arXiv preprint dated 16 June 2026, Shakiba, Rokni, Mohammadi, and Dehghani initialize recurrent weights from nearly 12,000 coregistered excitatory neurons and impose communication-aware spatial constraints while training on three cognitive decision-making tasks.
ocar.resolution: Networks constrained by cortical structure and function outperform baseline and partial constraints. Functional weight initialization provides the largest gain; real spatial embedding adds robust further improvement. Learned nets show low-entropy, modular, small-world organization and remain strong even when recurrence is restricted to positive weights. Code is pointed to github.com/neurovium/CorticalBlueprintRNN.
ocar.future_work: The authors present cortex’s geometry, wiring, and function as a practical inductive basis for RNNs; tasks are cognitive benchmarks, not the animals’ visual behaviors.

summaries.beginner: A mouse visual-cortex dataset that includes both wiring and activity can be used as a recipe for artificial recurrent networks. This study finds that starting from real functional relationships, then respecting where cells sit in space, helps those networks learn faster and look more brain-like.
summaries.intermediate: In arXiv:2606.14975 (16 June 2026), Shakiba, Rokni, Mohammadi, and Dehghani build RNNs from MICrONS mouse visual cortex: spatial coordinates, EM connectivity, and function-derived relations among nearly 12,000 coregistered excitatory neurons, with communication-aware spatial penalties during learning. Across three cognitive decision-making tasks, full structure-and-function constraints beat baselines; functional initialization is the largest single gain, with real spatial embedding adding further improvement. Networks become modular and small-world with low entropy, and performance holds under excitatory-only recurrence.
summaries.advanced: Units are excitatory neurons only; inhibition is not taken from the EM graph in the stated setup. Tasks are cognitive decision-making benchmarks, not MICrONS visual stimuli. “Outperform” is reported without numeric scores in the extract used here. Spatial constraints follow prior seRNN work; gains could partly reflect sparsity rather than mouse-specific geometry. Catalog dimension is image-acquisition, but the paper is a modeling/ML study on already released MICrONS data.

plain_language_summary: A mouse visual-cortex dataset that includes both wiring and activity can be used as a recipe for artificial recurrent networks. This study finds that starting from real functional relationships, then respecting where cells sit in space, helps those networks learn faster and look more brain-like.

ocar.opportunity: Multimodal, multiscale brain atlases now exist across species, but molecular, morphological, and activity data are hard to analyze together in one 3D reference space.
ocar.challenge: Heterogeneous file types and scales (insects to primates; light versus electron microscopy) lack a shared representation for interactive, source-independent queries.
ocar.action: On bioRxiv (version posted 25 March 2026), Wang, Chen, Wei, Ma, Zhong, Li, Jin, Cheng, Guan, Zheng, Zhang, Chen, Zheng, Xu, Wang, Du, and Du present iBrAVE, an open-source ParaView-based platform that unifies datasets into five core representations.
ocar.resolution: Single-modality tools include spatially resolved single-neuron morphology (geometry, topology, projection, clustering, putative wiring). Cross-modal tools link gene expression and activity to morphologically defined neurons via spatial correspondence. Cross-scale tools infer identity and synaptic connectivity between light- and electron-microscopy reconstructions by morphology matching. Code is at github.com/soaringdu/Proj-iBrAVE; docs at zebrafish.cn/iBrAVE.
ocar.future_work: Limitations include unquantified registration uncertainty, lack of native import for true single-cell multimodal ground truth, and the need for a plugin API so new analyses are not hard-coded.

summaries.beginner: Brain atlases now mix genes, cell shapes, activity, and electron-microscope wiring, but they live in different files. This software puts them in one 3D space so researchers can click from a neuron’s shape to nearby genes or to a matching EM cell.
summaries.intermediate: In a bioRxiv preprint (doi 10.1101/2025.10.04.680445, posted 25 March 2026), Wang, Du, Du, and colleagues introduce iBrAVE, an open-source 3D platform (built on ParaView 5.12.0) for integrative atlas analysis from insects to primates. Datasets are unified into five core representations. Demonstrations include morphology analytics, spatial linking of gene expression and activity to identified neurons, and bidirectional light-microscopy versus EM identity/synapse inference via morphology matching. Documentation and tutorials are hosted at zebrafish.cn/iBrAVE.
summaries.advanced: This is a preprint methods/software paper. Cross-modal links depend on registration quality; the authors say uncertainty is not yet visualized. Putative wiring from LM morphology is not EM-verified connectivity unless a match is made. Plugin-style analytics still require code integration. Species coverage is as imported, not a new atlas. Catalog tags electron microscopy, but the contribution is infrastructure spanning modalities.

plain_language_summary: Brain atlases now mix genes, cell shapes, activity, and electron-microscope wiring, but they live in different files. This software puts them in one 3D space so researchers can click from a neuron’s shape to nearby genes or to a matching EM cell.

ocar.opportunity: Deep EM neuron segmentation still over-fragments large, thin arbors, so automatic detection of which fragments should merge is a core proofreading bottleneck.
ocar.challenge: Local image context cannot see millimeter-scale morphology, while naive comparison of all adjacent fragments does not scale; fly central-brain neurons average 2.15 mm with radii down to about 100 nm, and flood-filling networks can yield up to a hundred fragments per cell.
ocar.action: In IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging (May 2026), Chen, Chen, Wang, Xiong, and Wu propose a connection-point detector that fuses global 3D morphology with high-resolution local EM via proposal-based sampling and multimodal cross-attention, then a second multimodal network that predicts whether to merge.
ocar.resolution: The combined pipeline is described as fully automatic neuron-segment merging that imitates human proofreading. Experiments are reported to verify the modules and robustness on large-scale reconstruction. Code and data: https://github.com/Levishery/Neuron-Segment-Connection-Prediction.
ocar.future_work: The method addresses split errors (oversegmentation), not an end-to-end replacement for all merge-error and synapse-proofreading tasks.

summaries.beginner: Computers often chop one neuron into many pieces in electron-microscope stacks. This paper looks at both the big 3D shape of those pieces and the close-up pictures at the join, then decides which pieces belong together, the way a human proofreader would.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TMI (May 2026, 45(5):2574ff), Chen, Chen, Wang, Xiong, and Wu target automatic merge of oversegmented EM neuron fragments. A connection-point detection network combines global 3D morphological features with local high-resolution image context; proposal-based sampling makes multimodal cross-attention tractable across scale. A second multimodal connectivity network decides merges, forming a full automatic pipeline. Motivating statistics include FAFB-scale fly neurons of mean length 2.15 mm and about 100 nm minimum radius, with FFN producing up to about 100 fragments per neuron. Code is released on GitHub.
summaries.advanced: The extract’s discussion is mostly references; quantitative benchmark scores are not taken from this selected text. Motivating fragment counts cite FFN/FAFB literature. The pipeline imitates human split-correction, not full proofreading (merge errors, synapses). Fusion quality depends on proposal recall: missed connection points never reach the second net. IEEE download stamp in the PDF is incidental to the science.

plain_language_summary: Computers often chop one neuron into many pieces in electron-microscope stacks. This paper looks at both the big 3D shape of those pieces and the close-up pictures at the join, then decides which pieces belong together, the way a human proofreader would.
